blocks.text: Credentials, tokens and keys leak through client-side JavaScript and source maps, public repositories and their history, build artifacts, container layers, mobile app packages, logs and error pages. A leaked secret often gives direct access to a cloud account, a database, a payment or messaging provider, or an internal API, so exposure is high impact even when the bug itself is simple. This category lists detection patterns and search commands, not credentials.

items: Secrets embedded in bundled JavaScript, source maps and HTML comments
Configuration and environment files, backups and VCS history exposed on the web
Committed keys in repositories, forks, gists, issues and CI logs
Keys in mobile apps, desktop installers and container image layers
Verbose errors and debug pages that print connection strings and tokens
Pre-signed URLs and tokens with excessive lifetime or scope
Third-party secrets in public API documentation and Postman collections

blocks.text: Collect JavaScript, source maps and public repository content within your scope, then search with the patterns here. Treat every match as a lead and confirm the format and context by reading the code around it. Do not use a discovered credential beyond the minimum your program allows to show that it is live (many programs prohibit any use); never access customer data, never copy secrets into reports in full, and redact all but the first few characters. Report the location, the type, the exposure period if known, and the rotation advice. Rotate a secret as soon as it has been found.

See `secrets-exposure-patterns.txt` for regular expressions, search commands and exposure locations. The file contains patterns and formats only; it must not contain real or realistic-looking credentials.
